lessons.title: The Carbon Paradox: Launching the Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: Before any demonstration, a student wrote: "Both samples are 100% carbon with the same number of protons, neutrons and electrons, so both will leave the same mark on a ceramic tile and both will light a bulb." After the scratch test and the conductivity test, what can be said about this prediction?
choices: It was supported by the scratch test but not by the conductivity test
It cannot be checked, because predictions are never compared with observations
It was supported, because both samples behaved in the same way in both tests
It was not supported, because the two samples behaved differently in both tests
quiz.rationale: Graphite smeared grey while diamond scratched the tile, and graphite lit the bulb while diamond did not. The samples differed in both tests, so the prediction of identical behaviour was not supported.
quiz.placement: Predict phase: annotating the original three predictions after the demonstrations (circle matches, cross out mismatches)

quiz.prompt: In the scratch test, a graphite stick and a diamond chip were each pressed firmly across a white ceramic tile. Which description records only what was observed?
choices: Diamond left a grey smear, while graphite left a white scratch in the tile
Both samples left a grey smear and the tile was not damaged
Graphite left a broad grey smear, while diamond left a white scratch in the tile itself
Neither sample left any mark on the tile
quiz.rationale: The graphite smeared grey on the tile, while the diamond gouged a white scratch into the tile surface and was itself undamaged.
quiz.placement: Observe phase: Demo 1 — Scratch Test on the ceramic tile

quiz.prompt: A simple 6 V battery-and-bulb conductivity tester was touched to a graphite stick and then to a diamond chip. What was observed?
choices: The bulb did not light with either sample
The bulb lit brightly with graphite but did not light at all with diamond
The bulb lit with diamond but did not light with graphite
The bulb lit with both samples
quiz.rationale: Graphite completed the circuit and the bulb lit brightly. Diamond did not light the bulb at all.
quiz.placement: Observe phase: Demo 2 — Conductivity Test with the bulb-and-battery tester

quiz.prompt: Students were told to write observations in the Observation Table, not explanations. Which of these statements is an observation rather than an explanation?
choices: The bulb lit because graphite is black and so it is a better material
The bulb lit because graphite is cheaper than diamond
The bulb did not light because diamond is too shiny
The bulb lit when the probes touched the graphite stick
quiz.rationale: Saying that the bulb lit when the probes touched graphite describes what the eyes saw. The other statements use "because" to give a reason that the demonstration did not show.
quiz.placement: Observe phase: completing the structured Observation Table (Property | Diamond | Graphite | My Surprise Rating)

quiz.prompt: Both the diamond chip and the graphite stick were labelled "100% Carbon — no other elements." Which statement best describes the puzzle the class was left with?
choices: The two samples behaved differently because one was a solid and the other was not
The diamond must contain an extra element that the graphite does not have
The graphite must contain more protons than the diamond
Two samples made only of carbon behaved very differently in hardness, conduction and appearance, and the class cannot yet explain why
quiz.rationale: The paradox is that two pure-carbon samples showed very different properties. At this stage no group has a complete explanation, which is what makes it a puzzle. The other choices are misconceptions that the labels contradict.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Group Explanation Attempt and gallery walk

quiz.prompt: During the Group Explanation Attempt, the teacher said: "A good scientific explanation attempt is one that is logical and based on evidence — not one that is correct." Which explanation attempt best fits this advice?
choices: Refusing to write anything until the correct answer is known
A paragraph that uses the scratch and conductivity observations as evidence and is honest about what it cannot yet explain
Copying the answer from a textbook without using the observation table
Choosing whichever idea most students in the class like best
quiz.rationale: A good attempt links reasoning to the observed evidence, even if it is incomplete. Copying, refusing to try or voting does not use the evidence.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: Group Explanation Attempt written in groups of 4

quiz.prompt: Students posted questions on the Driving Question Board (DQB) that the demonstration raised but did NOT answer. Which question belongs on the DQB?
choices: What colour was the sticky note I used?
Does the graphite stick make the bulb light?
I wonder why diamond scratches the tile but graphite only leaves a smear
Was the graphite stick taken from an HB pencil?
quiz.rationale: A good DQB question is about the phenomenon and is still unanswered. The question about the bulb was answered by the demonstration, the HB pencil was stated in the lesson, and the sticky note colour has nothing to do with the puzzle.
quiz.placement: DQB phase: writing one question per sticky note and posting them on the Driving Question Board

quiz.prompt: At the end of the lesson, each student draws an Initial Model of the carbon atoms inside diamond and graphite, signs and dates it, and the models are stored in Model Envelopes. Why are the models kept?
choices: So students can compare them with their final model at the end of the unit and see how their thinking has changed
So they can be marked for correctness in this lesson
So the class can copy the best drawing as the right answer
So they can be thrown away once the DQB is complete
quiz.rationale: The envelope holds a "before" model so that growth in understanding can be seen when it is returned at the end of the unit. The drawings are not marked as right or wrong today.
quiz.placement: Model phase: drawing the Initial Model and storing it in the Model Envelope

lessons.title: Valence Electrons & the Octet Rule: The Electron Bookkeeping Behind the Carbon Paradox

quiz.prompt: Carbon has atomic number 6. Which choice correctly gives its electron configuration and the number of electrons that take part in bonding (valence electrons)?
choices: Configuration 6; 6 valence electrons
Configuration 2,4; 6 valence electrons
Configuration 2,4; 2 valence electrons
Configuration 2,4; 4 valence electrons
quiz.rationale: Six electrons fill shell 1 (2) and then shell 2 (4), giving 2,4. Only the 4 electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons; the 2 inner electrons do not bond.
quiz.placement: Predict: write carbon's electron configuration and circle the bonding electrons

quiz.prompt: A chlorine atom has atomic number 17, so its electron configuration is 2,8,7. How many valence electrons does it have?
quiz.rationale: Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell only. Working: 17 - 2 - 8 = 7, which matches the 7 in the third shell. Counting all 17 electrons is the common error of including inner-shell electrons.
quiz.placement: Part: 'Mapping Outer Electrons Across Periods 1-3' worksheet and the chlorine finger-check

quiz.prompt: Across Period 2 (Li to Ne) the number of valence electrons goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Why does the count go back to 1 at sodium (Na, 2,8,1)?
choices: Sodium is a noble gas, so it starts again
Sodium has lost seven of its electrons
Sodium starts filling a new third shell, which holds one electron
Sodium has only one electron altogether
quiz.rationale: Neon's second shell is full (2,8). Sodium's 11th electron must go into a new third shell, so it has 1 valence electron. The pattern repeats in each new period.
quiz.placement: Class discussion: 'What do you notice about where this sequence resets?'

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the octet rule and the duplet rule?
choices: Period 1 atoms need 8 electrons, and Period 2 atoms need 2
Atoms react to get 8 valence electrons, or 2 for Period 1 atoms such as hydrogen, matching the nearest noble gas
All atoms need exactly 8 electrons in total, including inner shells
Atoms with 8 valence electrons react very easily to lose them
quiz.rationale: The octet rule says atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 valence electrons, like a noble gas. Period 1 has only one shell, which holds 2 electrons (duplet rule).
quiz.placement: Matatu analogy and the board statement 'OCTET RULE'

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct Lewis dot diagram for a nitrogen atom (atomic number 7, configuration 2,5)?
choices: Seven dots spread around the symbol, all in pairs except one
Five dots: one dot on each of the four sides, then the fifth paired with one of them
Five dots, all drawn on one side of the symbol
Three dots, one on each of three sides
quiz.rationale: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons. Dots go one per side first (4 dots), and the fifth is paired with one of them. This gives one pair and three unpaired dots.
quiz.placement: Mini-whiteboard practice: drawing Lewis dot diagrams for N, O, F, Ne and Period 3 elements

quiz.prompt: A carbon atom has 4 valence electrons shown as 4 unpaired dots. What does this tell us about the number of bonds carbon can form?
choices: 2 bonds, because only half of the dots can be shared
6 bonds, because carbon has 6 electrons altogether
8 bonds, because it wants to have an octet
4 bonds, because it needs 4 more electrons to complete its octet by sharing
quiz.rationale: Each unpaired valence electron can be shared in a bond. Carbon has 4 and needs 4 more to reach 8, so it can form four bonds. This is why carbon is so versatile.
quiz.placement: Carbon Lewis dot diagram question: 'What does that tell us about how many bonds it can form?'

quiz.prompt: A sodium atom has configuration 2,8,1. What is the easiest way for it to reach a full outer shell like a noble gas?
choices: Lose all 11 electrons
Gain 7 electrons to make a full third shell
Share 4 electrons with another atom
Lose its 1 outer electron so that its full second shell becomes the outer shell
quiz.rationale: Losing one electron leaves sodium with configuration 2,8, a full outer shell like neon. Gaining 7 electrons would take far more change than losing 1.
quiz.placement: Matatu analogy question: 'How many electrons does ... sodium need to gain, lose, or share?'

lessons.title: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer and the Giant Ionic Structure

quiz.prompt: Sodium (electron arrangement 2,8,1) reacts with chlorine (electron arrangement 2,8,7) to form sodium chloride, NaCl. Which statement correctly describes what happens to the electrons?
choices: Sodium and chlorine atoms share one pair of electrons equally
Chlorine transfers one electron to sodium
Both atoms lose their outer electrons and the electrons float freely between them
Sodium transfers its one outer electron to chlorine
quiz.rationale: Sodium is a metal with one valence electron and chlorine is a non-metal needing one more electron. The outer electron moves completely from Na to Cl, giving each a full outer shell. Sharing is a common misconception for ionic bonding.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Electron Transfer Card Model

quiz.prompt: A sodium atom has the electron arrangement 2,8,1. It loses its one outer electron to form a sodium ion. Which row correctly gives the ion's symbol and electron arrangement?
choices: Na⁻ with 2,8
Na⁺ with 2,8,1
Na⁺ with 2,8
Na⁻ with 2,8,2
quiz.rationale: Losing one negative electron leaves one more proton than electrons, so the charge is 1+. The remaining electrons are arranged 2,8, a full outer shell.
quiz.placement: Activity A — Electron Transfer Card Model (labelling the ion charges Na⁺ and Cl⁻)

quiz.prompt: A chlorine atom has 17 protons and 17 electrons. After it receives one electron from a sodium atom, it becomes a chloride ion. Why does the chloride ion have a charge of 1−?
choices: It has lost a proton, so the positive charge is reduced
It has the same number of protons and electrons, but the electrons are arranged differently
It has 17 electrons and 18 protons, so the charge is negative
It has 18 electrons but only 17 protons, so there is one extra negative charge
quiz.rationale: Gaining one electron gives 18 electrons (2,8,8) and still 17 protons. One extra negative charge means the overall charge is 1−.
quiz.placement: Activity B — Simulation, pause (ii): just after transfer (ions formed)

quiz.prompt: Magnesium (Group 2) reacts with oxygen (Group 6) to form magnesium oxide, MgO, which is used to line furnaces. Which description of the dot-and-cross diagram for MgO is correct?
choices: Mg and O share 2 pairs of electrons and no ions form
O transfers 2 electrons to Mg, forming Mg²⁻ and O²⁺
Mg transfers 2 electrons to O, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, each with 8 electrons in its outer shell
Mg transfers 1 electron to O, forming Mg⁺ and O⁻
quiz.rationale: Mg has 2 valence electrons and O has 6. Mg gives away 2 electrons to O, so Mg becomes Mg²⁺ and O becomes O²⁻, and both have full outer shells of 8 electrons.
quiz.placement: Part A — Dot-and-Cross Diagrams (independent MgO diagram)

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes lattice energy?
choices: The energy released when two atoms share a pair of electrons
The energy needed to remove one electron from a sodium atom
The energy needed to make chlorine atoms form a gas
The energy released when gaseous ions pack together to form a giant ionic lattice
quiz.rationale: Lattice energy is the energy released when separated gaseous ions come together into a lattice. It explains why ionic compounds are stable and why a lot of energy is needed to pull the lattice apart.
quiz.placement: Part B — Conceptual Lattice Energy (Nairobi City Market analogy)

quiz.prompt: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride and sodium chloride solution do. What is the reason?
choices: Sodium chloride is made of molecules that only separate when heated or dissolved
Free electrons move through solid sodium chloride but are trapped when it melts
Melting or dissolving adds extra electrons to the sodium chloride
In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions, but when molten or dissolved the ions are free to move and carry charge
quiz.rationale: Electrical conduction in ionic compounds needs charged particles that can move. In the solid lattice the ions cannot move, but they can when the compound is molten or dissolved in water.
quiz.placement: Part C — Property Prediction Table (electrical conductivity as solid / as solution / when molten)

quiz.prompt: Learners build a model of part of a sodium chloride lattice using maize kernels for Na⁺ ions and beans for Cl⁻ ions. They place the maize and beans alternately in a checkerboard pattern. Why is this alternating arrangement correct?
choices: Each ion is attracted to ions of the same charge, so like ions must touch
Each ion is attracted to neighbouring ions of opposite charge, which holds the lattice together strongly in all directions
The ions alternate only to make the lattice look neat; it has no effect on the forces between them
Alternating ions make pairs of molecules that are joined by shared electrons
quiz.rationale: In a giant ionic lattice each Na⁺ is surrounded by Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by Na⁺ ions. Strong electrostatic attraction between opposite charges acts in all directions, which explains the high melting point.
quiz.placement: Bonding Concept Model — Ionic Bonding panel (maize and beans 2-D lattice cross-section)

lessons.title: Covalent & Dative Covalent Bonding: Drawing Lewis Structures and Exploring Electron Sharing

quiz.prompt: Carbon has the electron arrangement 2,4. Using this, how many covalent bonds can one carbon atom form to reach a stable noble gas arrangement?
quiz.rationale: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and needs 8 for a full outer shell, so it shares 4 electrons by forming 4 covalent bonds (8 - 4 = 4).
quiz.placement: Predict Card (B): how many bonds can one carbon atom form

quiz.prompt: In an oxygen molecule (O₂) the two atoms share a double bond. Each oxygen atom has 6 valence electrons. How many lone pairs does each oxygen atom have in O₂?
quiz.rationale: Each oxygen shares 2 of its electrons in the double bond, leaving 6 - 2 = 4 non-bonding electrons, which is 2 lone pairs.
quiz.placement: Activity A: ARES simulation and Observation Table (O₂ double bond, lone pairs per atom)

quiz.prompt: Which description of a correct dot-and-cross diagram for methane (CH₄) is right?
choices: Carbon has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, and only 2 hydrogens are attached
Carbon has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, and each hydrogen shares 1 pair
Carbon has 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, and each hydrogen has 8 electrons
Carbon transfers 4 electrons to 4 hydrogen atoms to form ions
quiz.rationale: Carbon shares its 4 valence electrons with 4 hydrogen atoms, giving 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs. Each hydrogen has 2 electrons, like helium.
quiz.placement: Activity B: guided dot-and-cross construction, board pass check for CH₄

quiz.prompt: In the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺), a hydrogen ion (H⁺, which has no electrons) joins an NH₃ molecule. Which statement correctly describes the new N–H bond?
choices: The hydrogen ion donates both electrons of the shared pair to nitrogen
Nitrogen transfers one electron completely to the hydrogen ion
Nitrogen donates both electrons of its lone pair to form the shared pair
Nitrogen and the hydrogen ion each give one electron to the shared pair
quiz.rationale: H⁺ has no electrons, so nitrogen supplies both electrons of the shared pair from its lone pair. This is a dative covalent bond.
quiz.placement: Part A: dative covalent bonds (NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺)

quiz.prompt: After the dative bond has formed in NH₄⁺, how does it compare with the other three N–H bonds in the ion?
choices: It is weaker, because only one atom supplied the electrons
It is stronger, because nitrogen gave both electrons
It is identical to the others; the arrow only shows where the electrons came from
It is ionic, because nitrogen has donated electrons
quiz.rationale: Once formed, a dative covalent bond is the same as an ordinary covalent bond. The arrow only records the origin of the shared pair.
quiz.placement: Part A: teacher's explanation of the dative bond arrow in NH₄⁺

quiz.prompt: In graphite each carbon atom forms 3 covalent bonds in a flat hexagonal layer. Which statement correctly explains why graphite conducts electricity?
choices: Graphite contains positive and negative ions that move when a current flows
Each carbon uses 3 of its 4 valence electrons in bonds, and the 4th is delocalised and free to move
Each carbon forms 4 bonds, so extra electrons are pushed out of the layer
Each carbon has a lone pair that moves between the layers
quiz.rationale: Three of carbon's 4 valence electrons are in bonding pairs. The 4th electron is not held in a bond; it is delocalised and carries charge through the layers.
quiz.placement: Part B: Bonding Comparison Card, why graphite conducts but diamond cannot

quiz.prompt: In diamond each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds in a 3-D tetrahedral network. Why is diamond an electrical insulator?
choices: Diamond contains ions that are locked in position
All 4 valence electrons of every carbon are held in bonding pairs, so none are free to move
Diamond is too hard for electrons to pass through
Diamond carbon atoms have lone pairs that cannot move
quiz.rationale: Each carbon uses all 4 valence electrons in four bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons to carry charge.
quiz.placement: Covalent bonding panel: diamond tetrahedral unit labelled 'no free electrons → insulator'

quiz.prompt: Which pair of statements correctly compares sodium chloride (ionic) with methane (covalent)?
choices: Both NaCl and CH₄ form by sharing electrons, but NaCl shares more pairs
In NaCl electrons are transferred to form ions, and in CH₄ electrons are shared in pairs
Both NaCl and CH₄ form by transferring electrons, but CH₄ makes bigger ions
In NaCl electrons are shared, and in CH₄ electrons are transferred
quiz.rationale: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming ions in a lattice. In methane, carbon and hydrogen atoms share electron pairs to form discrete molecules.
quiz.placement: Part C: dot-and-cross comparison of NaCl and covalent diagrams (T-chart IONIC | COVALENT)

lessons.title: Hydrogen Bonding & Van der Waals Forces: Why Water Defies Expectation

quiz.prompt: The boiling points of three Group VI hydrides are: H₂Te −2 °C, H₂Se −41 °C, H₂S −60 °C. The boiling point falls as the molecules get smaller. If water (H₂O, the smallest of these molecules) followed this same trend, what boiling point would you expect?
choices: About −41 °C, the same as H₂Se
Lower than −60 °C, roughly −80 °C
About 0 °C, the freezing point of water
About 100 °C, because water is a very common liquid
quiz.rationale: The trend shows boiling point dropping as molecules get smaller, so extending it to the smallest molecule (H₂O) gives a value below −60 °C. The real value of 100 °C is an anomaly, which is the puzzle for the lesson.
quiz.placement: Predict: Group VI hydride boiling point table and trend-line prediction

quiz.prompt: A few iodine crystals in a flask are gently warmed in a water bath at about 50 °C. Purple vapour forms directly from the solid, with almost no liquid seen. What is this change of state called?
choices: Melting followed by boiling
Evaporation of a liquid
Sublimation
Condensation
quiz.rationale: A solid changing directly into a gas without passing through the liquid state is sublimation. Saying iodine 'melted' is the red flag the teacher looks for.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Iodine Sublimation Demonstration

quiz.prompt: Xenon (Xe) atoms have 54 electrons and the substance boils at −108 °C. Iodine (I₂) molecules have 106 electrons and the substance boils at 184 °C. Neither substance can form hydrogen bonds. What best explains why iodine boils so much higher than xenon?
choices: The larger electron cloud of I₂ is easier to distort, so its London dispersion forces are stronger
The covalent bond inside I₂ is stronger than anything holding Xe atoms together, so more energy is needed to boil I₂
Xenon atoms attract one another more strongly because they are single atoms
I₂ forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules
quiz.rationale: More electrons mean a larger electron cloud that is more easily distorted into temporary dipoles. This gives stronger London dispersion forces between I₂ molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them. Boiling does not break the covalent bond inside I₂.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Boiling Point Data Analysis (comparing iodine with xenon)

quiz.prompt: Hydrogen bonding can form between molecules when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom. Which of these substances has molecules that can form hydrogen bonds with each other?
choices: Argon (Ar)
Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S)
Water (H₂O)
Hydrogen chloride (HCl)
quiz.rationale: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F. Only water has H bonded to one of these (oxygen). Sulfur and chlorine are not electronegative enough in the way the lesson rule requires, and argon has no hydrogen.
quiz.placement: Part A: Hydrogen Bonding (rule: H bonded to N, O or F; comparing water with H₂S)

quiz.prompt: Two water molecules are drawn next to each other. Where does the hydrogen bond between them form?
choices: Between the two hydrogen atoms of the same molecule, shown as a solid line
Between a hydrogen atom of one molecule and a hydrogen atom of the other molecule
Between the two oxygen atoms, one from each molecule
Between the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and a lone pair on the δ− oxygen of the neighbouring molecule, shown as a dashed line
quiz.rationale: A hydrogen bond is a weak electrostatic attraction between the δ+ H of one molecule and a lone pair on the δ− O of a neighbouring molecule. It is drawn as a dashed line, not a solid covalent bond.
quiz.placement: Part A: Hydrogen Bonding (diagram of three water molecules, and the exit mini-task of drawing one hydrogen bond)

quiz.prompt: Graphite has flat layers of carbon atoms. Within each layer the atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. Why can the layers slide over each other so that graphite is soft and leaves a mark on paper?
choices: The covalent bonds between the layers are weak because carbon atoms are large
Only weak Van der Waals forces hold the layers together, and these are much weaker than the covalent bonds within the layers
The layers are held together by strong hydrogen bonds that let them move
The covalent bonds inside each layer break easily when you press on graphite
quiz.rationale: Between the layers there are only weak Van der Waals forces, so the layers slide easily. Diamond has no such weak links because its 3-D network is covalently bonded throughout.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: green sticky note connecting intermolecular forces to graphite

quiz.prompt: You are drawing a particle model of graphite. Which drawing convention correctly shows the forces inside and between the layers?
choices: Dashed lines between carbon atoms within each layer, and solid lines between the layers
Solid lines for covalent bonds within each hexagonal layer, and dashed lines between the layers labelled weak Van der Waals forces
Solid lines between the layers, labelled as strong covalent bonds, to show that the layers are firmly joined
Hydrogen bonds drawn as dashed lines between the layers
quiz.rationale: Strong covalent bonds inside each layer are drawn as solid lines. The weak Van der Waals forces between the layers are drawn as dashed lines. Mixing these up confuses forces within layers with forces between layers.
quiz.placement: Cumulative particle model of carbon structures: revising the graphite portion

lessons.title: Metallic Bonding: The Sea of Electrons — From Copper Wire to Aluminium Foil

quiz.prompt: In sodium chloride the electrons are transferred, and in water they are shared between two specific atoms. In a piece of aluminium foil, where every atom is the same element, what is the best description of what happens to the outer (valence) electrons?
choices: They are released into a shared pool and move freely throughout the whole structure
They stay on their own aluminium atom and do not move
They are transferred from one aluminium atom to another aluminium atom and stay there
They are shared in pairs between two specific neighbouring aluminium atoms
quiz.rationale: In metallic bonding, atoms release their valence electrons into a pool of delocalised electrons that belong to no single ion. This is the model students meet in the explanation, and it corrects the 'electrons stay on their own atom' misconception.
quiz.placement: Predict: written prediction 'What do you predict happens to the electrons in a metal like aluminium?'

quiz.prompt: A conductivity tester (cells, torch bulb and two crocodile-clip leads) is used to test three solids in turn: aluminium foil, solid sodium chloride (NaCl) and candle wax. Which result is correct?
choices: The bulb lights for all three solids
The bulb lights for aluminium foil only
The bulb lights for aluminium foil and solid NaCl, but not for the candle wax
The bulb lights for solid NaCl only, because it contains ions
quiz.rationale: Aluminium has delocalised electrons that carry charge. Solid NaCl has ions locked in the lattice and candle wax is a simple molecular substance with no free charged particles, so neither conducts.
quiz.placement: Demonstration step (3): conductivity tester on aluminium foil, solid NaCl and candle wax

quiz.prompt: Using the sea-of-electrons model, which statement best explains why metals conduct electricity?
choices: Metals contain negative ions that are attracted to the battery
The positive metal ions are free to move through the wire and carry the current
Electrons are held in fixed positions between pairs of atoms and pass the charge along
The delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge when a voltage is applied
quiz.rationale: The positive ions stay in the lattice. The delocalised electrons move freely throughout the metal and carry charge when a voltage is applied.
quiz.placement: Step 4, Question A: 'Using the sea-of-electrons model, explain why metals conduct electricity'

quiz.prompt: A copper wire is bent into a curve and does not break, while a salt crystal would shatter if struck. Which statement best explains why the copper wire does not break?
choices: The layers of ions cannot move at all, so the wire only appears to bend
Sliding the layers brings positive ions next to each other, but the repulsion is too weak to matter
The bonds between particular pairs of copper atoms break and then reform in the new position
The sea of electrons surrounds the ions in all directions, so there is no directional bond to break and the attraction continues when the ions slide
quiz.rationale: Metallic bonding is non-directional. The electron sea keeps attracting the ions after the layers slide, whereas in an ionic crystal sliding brings like charges together and the crystal cracks.
quiz.placement: Step 4, Question B: 'When we bend copper wire, the layers of positive ions slide past each other but the wire does not break. Why not?'

quiz.prompt: Metals such as iron (melting point 1538 °C) have much higher melting points than iodine (114 °C). Which statement best explains this using the metallic bonding model?
choices: Iron has weak forces between its particles, but they are packed more closely than in iodine
There are many positive ions and many delocalised electrons, so the strong electrostatic attraction between them needs a lot of energy to overcome
Iron has only a few positive ions, so they are held together tightly
Iron atoms are joined in pairs by covalent bonds, and these bonds are very hard to break
quiz.rationale: Strong electrostatic attraction between the lattice of positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons requires much energy to overcome. This is a stronger interaction than the forces between iodine molecules.
quiz.placement: Step 4, Question C: 'Why do metals generally have high melting points compared to simple molecular substances like iodine?'

quiz.prompt: A student must draw a labelled 2-D diagram of metallic bonding in aluminium. Which diagram is correct?
choices: A regular grid of positive aluminium ions with a cloud of small dots, labelled delocalised electrons, around and between all the ions
A grid of neutral atoms, each with its own electrons kept inside its own circle
A grid of alternating positive and negative ions, with no electrons shown
Two aluminium atoms joined by a shared pair of dots and crosses between them
quiz.rationale: A correct diagram has labelled positive ions in a lattice and the delocalised electrons shown as a cloud or distributed dots. The other options show covalent-style sharing, an ionic lattice, or electrons that are not delocalised.
quiz.placement: Step 3 board diagram: 4x4 grid of circles with a cloud of dots labelled 'delocalised electrons (sea of electrons)'

quiz.prompt: Graphite is a covalent solid made only of carbon, yet it conducts electricity. Using what you have learned about delocalised electrons, which explanation is best?
choices: Each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layer and carry charge
Each carbon atom is held in a fixed bond by all four of its electrons, which lets charge pass
Graphite conducts because the carbon atoms are packed in a 3-D tetrahedral network
Graphite contains positive and negative ions that move when a voltage is applied
quiz.rationale: In graphite each carbon forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move in the layer. A 3-D network where all four electrons are held in bonds, as in diamond, does not conduct.
quiz.placement: DQB update: linking delocalised electrons to the graphite conductivity question from Lesson 1

quiz.prompt: Which row of the 'Three Bond Types' summary table correctly describes how electrons behave in each type of bonding?
choices: Ionic: electrons shared between two atoms. Covalent: electrons transferred. Metallic: electrons delocalised
Ionic: electrons transferred from metal to non-metal. Covalent: electrons shared between two specific atoms. Metallic: electrons delocalised in a sea
Ionic: electrons delocalised. Covalent: electrons transferred. Metallic: electrons shared between two specific atoms
Ionic: electrons transferred. Covalent: electrons delocalised. Metallic: electrons shared between two specific atoms
quiz.rationale: Ionic bonding involves complete transfer of electrons, covalent bonding involves sharing between specific atoms, and metallic bonding involves delocalised electrons moving throughout the lattice.
quiz.placement: Three-column table 'Three Bond Types — Evidence Summary' (BOND TYPE / HOW ELECTRONS BEHAVE / PROPERTIES EXPLAINED)

lessons.title: Physical Properties Investigation — Part 1: Setup & Prediction

quiz.prompt: Two white crystalline solids look alike: table salt (NaCl) and white sugar. Which statement classifies them correctly by structure and bonding?
choices: NaCl is a simple molecular structure; sugar is a giant ionic structure
Both are simple molecular structures because both dissolve in water
Both are giant ionic structures because both are white crystals
NaCl is a giant ionic structure; sugar is a simple molecular structure
quiz.rationale: NaCl is a lattice of oppositely charged ions (giant ionic). Sugar is made of separate covalently bonded molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces (simple molecular). Appearance alone cannot decide the structure type.
quiz.placement: Individual prediction: Column 1 ('Predicted Structure Type') of the Evidence Prediction Table, Unknown A and Unknown B

quiz.prompt: A strip of aluminium foil is predicted to conduct electricity even as a solid. Which reason is correct?
choices: Its molecules are free to move and carry charge
It contains ions that are free to move through the solid
Its atoms share electrons in covalent bonds that hold all electrons tightly in place
Its delocalised electrons are free to move through the giant metallic structure
quiz.rationale: Metals have a giant metallic structure with delocalised electrons that move freely and carry charge. Aluminium has no mobile ions or separate molecules in the solid.
quiz.placement: Individual prediction: Column 1 ('Predicted Structure Type') of the Evidence Prediction Table, Unknown D (aluminium foil pellet)

quiz.prompt: Sand (silicon dioxide, a giant covalent structure) has a melting point far higher than sugar (a simple molecular substance). What is the best particle-level explanation?
choices: Sand has stronger intermolecular forces between its molecules than sugar has
Sand is grey-white and sugar is white, so the colour makes the difference
Melting sand needs a huge amount of energy to break the many strong covalent bonds throughout the network, but melting sugar only needs weak forces between molecules to be overcome
Melting sugar breaks the covalent bonds inside each sugar molecule, which are weaker than the bonds in sand
quiz.rationale: In a giant covalent structure every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds that must be broken to melt it. In sugar only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome, so the melting point is much lower.
quiz.placement: Data Card matching task: matching melting points of Substance Type W, X, Y, Z to structural types and Unknowns A–D

quiz.prompt: A group predicts that solid NaCl will not light a bulb in a conductivity tester, but that a solution of NaCl in water will. What reason should they give?
choices: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice, but in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge
NaCl is a simple molecular substance, so only its solution conducts
In the solid there are no charged particles at all, but dissolving creates new ones
Water itself carries the current, so the NaCl does not matter
quiz.rationale: Conduction needs charged particles that are free and moving. Solid NaCl has ions locked in a lattice; dissolving frees them to move.
quiz.placement: Written predictions of electrical conductivity (solid, and dissolved or molten) for each structural type, with the prompt 'What would have to be free and moving?'

quiz.prompt: Kericho tea farmers dissolve fertiliser salts in water every season. Which of these four substances would you predict to dissolve in water in a similar way to a giant ionic fertiliser salt?
choices: Graphite from a pencil
Table salt (NaCl)
Fine dry sand (SiO₂)
Aluminium foil
quiz.rationale: NaCl is a giant ionic compound, like fertiliser salts, and is predicted to dissolve in water. Sand and graphite are giant covalent and aluminium is giant metallic, so none are predicted to dissolve.
quiz.placement: Circulating question: 'Kericho tea farmers dissolve fertiliser salts in water every season. Which of your unknowns do you predict will behave the same way?'

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both giant covalent structures made only of carbon. Which property is predicted to be different, and why?
choices: Electrical conductivity, because diamond contains free ions that graphite lacks
Solubility in water, because graphite dissolves as its layers are held by weak forces
Electrical conductivity, because each carbon in graphite uses three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron free to move between layers
Melting point, because graphite has no covalent bonds
quiz.rationale: Graphite carbon atoms form three bonds in flat layers, leaving one delocalised electron each that can move and carry charge. Diamond's four bonds per carbon leave no free electrons, so it does not conduct.
quiz.placement: Graphite discussion: targeted cold-call on which property differs for graphite versus diamond and sand (bonus unknowns E and F)

quiz.prompt: During a peer review, a group must choose the justification that gives particle-level REASONING for diamond's very high melting point, not just an observation. Which one is it?
choices: Diamond is very hard and sparkles
Diamond has a high melting point because it is a solid at room temperature
Diamond has a high melting point because the Nairobi jeweller's tool is made of it
Diamond has a high melting point because each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a 3-D network, and a lot of energy is needed to break these strong bonds
quiz.rationale: Good reasoning links bond type to structure to property. Only this choice names the covalent bonds, the 3-D network and the energy needed. The others only describe or restate observations.
quiz.placement: Peer review: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) protocol, circling cells where the justification is only an observation

quiz.prompt: Which learner's ORANGE card is the best testable claim linked to bond type for Lesson 8?
choices: Sand is grey-white and gritty.
How do we measure a melting point?
I think Unknown A will dissolve.
I predict that sand will not dissolve in water because it is a giant covalent structure with strong bonds throughout the network.
quiz.rationale: A good testable claim follows the format 'I predict that [substance] will [result] because [bond-type reason]'. The other choices are a bare guess, a procedural question and an observation.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: ORANGE card 'Testable Claim I am now confident about'

quiz.prompt: On the Property Prediction Ring of the Bonding Concept Model, a group fills in the Giant Covalent node for diamond and graphite. Which pair of predictions is correct?
choices: Both have a high melting point; diamond conducts electricity but graphite does not
Both have a high melting point, and both conduct electricity
Both have a high melting point; diamond does not conduct electricity but graphite does
Both have a low melting point; diamond does not conduct but graphite does
quiz.rationale: Both are giant covalent with strong bonds throughout, so both have high melting points. Only graphite has delocalised electrons, so only graphite is predicted to conduct. The two conductivity boxes must differ.
quiz.placement: Cumulative Bonding Concept Model: adding the Property Prediction Ring, Giant Covalent node (diamond and graphite)

lessons.title: Physical Properties Investigation — Part 2: Data Collection (Solubility, Conductivity & Melting Point)

quiz.prompt: A group tests sodium chloride (NaCl) with a conductivity tester. The bulb stays off when the probes touch solid NaCl, but it glows brightly when the probes are dipped in a NaCl solution. What has changed between the two tests?
choices: The water has added extra electrons to the NaCl
The NaCl has become a metal, so electrons can now flow
The sodium and chloride atoms have joined to form molecules
The ions in NaCl are now free to move in the water and carry charge
quiz.rationale: In solid NaCl the ions are locked in the lattice, so no charge can flow. When dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry current, so the bulb lights.
quiz.placement: Station B: Conductivity Testing (solid then dissolved)

quiz.prompt: Sugar (sucrose) is stirred into 50 mL of distilled water and dissolves completely. The conductivity tester is then dipped into the sugar solution. What result is expected?
choices: The bulb stays off because sugar did not dissolve
The bulb glows brightly, like NaCl solution, because sugar dissolved
The bulb stays off because sugar is a simple molecular compound and forms no free ions in solution
The bulb glows dimly because sugar is a metal
quiz.rationale: Sugar is a simple molecular compound. It dissolves as whole molecules, with no mobile ions or electrons, so the solution does not conduct.
quiz.placement: Station B: Conductivity Testing (dissolved samples) after Station A solubility results

quiz.prompt: Fine sand from a Kenyan river bed is mostly SiO₂, a giant covalent structure. A spatula of sand is stirred in 50 mL of water for 30 seconds. Which description best matches what is expected for SiO₂?
choices: It does not dissolve, but it melts easily
It does not dissolve, leaving a residue, and it has a very high melting point
It dissolves to form a clear solution and has a low melting point
It dissolves and conducts electricity in solution
quiz.rationale: Giant covalent structures such as SiO₂ are generally insoluble in water. Their strong covalent bonds throughout the structure give very high melting points.
quiz.placement: Station A: Solubility Testing (SiO₂ sand) and Station C: Melting Point Data Cards

quiz.prompt: A group tests five substances as solids with a conductivity tester: NaCl crystals, sugar crystals, dry SiO₂ sand and aluminium foil. Which one is expected to light the bulb in the solid state?
choices: Aluminium foil
NaCl crystals
Sugar crystals
Dry SiO₂ sand
quiz.rationale: Aluminium has a giant metallic structure with free-moving electrons, so it conducts when solid. The other three do not conduct as solids.
quiz.placement: Station B: Conductivity Testing (solid samples)

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Data cards show diamond has a melting point above 3,500 °C. Graphite does not melt at normal pressure and sublimes at about 3,650 °C. In the conductivity test, graphite lights the bulb but diamond does not. Which statement matches this evidence?
choices: Both conduct, because both are made of the same atoms
Graphite melts at a much lower temperature than diamond because it is soft
Diamond conducts and graphite does not, because diamond is harder
Both have extremely high melting points, but only graphite conducts electricity
quiz.rationale: Both carbon forms have extremely high melting points, but only graphite conducts. This is the carbon paradox: same atoms, different property.
quiz.placement: Station C: Melting Point Data Cards (diamond and graphite cards) and Station B critical connection

quiz.prompt: At Station B, a beaker of the water alone (with no substance dissolved) is tested with the conductivity tester as a control. Why is this control test done?
choices: To warm the probes before testing the other solutions
To dissolve any residue left on the probes
To show that all water conducts electricity better than solids
To make sure the bulb lighting with a solution is due to the dissolved substance and not the water itself
quiz.rationale: A control gives a baseline. If the water alone does not light the bulb, a bright bulb in a solution can be attributed to the dissolved substance.
quiz.placement: Station B: Conductivity Testing (beaker of water alone as a control)

quiz.prompt: From the class master table, a learner completes this Pattern Statement: 'Substances that conduct electricity in solution but not as solids seem to have ____ bonds.' Which word correctly fills the gap?
choices: Ionic
Metallic
Giant covalent
Simple molecular
quiz.rationale: Ionic compounds such as NaCl do not conduct as solids because their ions are fixed. They conduct in solution because the ions become free to move. Metals conduct as solids.
quiz.placement: Pattern Statement task, Starter 1 (after the master data table is built)

quiz.prompt: In the 'Giant Covalent' row of your model, you draw a two-cell table for diamond and graphite. Which entry best explains why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not?
choices: Diamond contains no carbon, while graphite does
In graphite, each carbon atom has one delocalised electron free to move between the layers. In diamond, all four outer electrons are held in bonds
Graphite has more protons in its atoms than diamond
Graphite is a metal, while diamond is a simple molecular compound
quiz.rationale: Graphite has three bonds per carbon atom in flat layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move. Diamond has four bonds per carbon atom in a 3-D network, so no electrons are free.
quiz.placement: Bonding Concept Model update: 'Giant Covalent' row, diamond/graphite two-cell sub-table

lessons.title: Physical Properties Investigation Part 3: Analysis, Explanation and DQB Update

quiz.prompt: Solid sodium chloride (NaCl) does not conduct electricity, but a solution of NaCl in water does. Which statement best explains this?
choices: In solution the NaCl forms small molecules that carry electric current
In the solid the delocalised electrons are trapped, but in water they are released
In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions, but in solution the ions are free to move and carry charge
In the solid there are no ions, but dissolving in water creates ions from nothing
quiz.rationale: NaCl is made of Na+ and Cl- ions held in a rigid lattice, so charge cannot flow. When dissolved (or molten) the ions are free to move and carry the current.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: whole-class compilation of the comparison table (NaCl conducts when dissolved)

quiz.prompt: Sugar does not conduct electricity as a solid or when dissolved in water. What does this tell us about sugar?
choices: It is an ionic compound whose ions cannot move in water
It is a giant metallic structure whose electrons are locked in place
It is a simple molecular substance made of neutral molecules, with no ions or free electrons to carry charge
It has delocalised electrons that are too weak to carry current
quiz.rationale: Sugar consists of neutral molecules, so it forms no ions in solution and has no free electrons. Therefore it cannot conduct in any state.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: teacher question to Wanjiku about sugar not conducting even in solution

quiz.prompt: Aluminium, used for mabati roofing, conducts electricity even as a solid. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Its positive ions are free to move through the solid
It contains Al+ and Cl- ions that move when heated
Its delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice of metal ions
Its atoms share electrons in pairs to form molecules that carry charge
quiz.rationale: Metals have a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. These electrons can move in the solid state and carry the current. Ions in a solid metal stay in fixed positions.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: sentence-frame scaffold for aluminium (giant metallic) and check on using 'delocalised electrons'

quiz.prompt: Sand (SiO2) is a giant covalent structure. Which pair of properties does it have, and why?
choices: It does not conduct and has a very high melting point, because it has no free ions or electrons and many strong covalent bonds must be broken
It conducts when solid and has a low melting point, because its electrons are free to move
It does not conduct and has a low melting point, because its molecules are held by weak forces
It conducts only when dissolved and has a high melting point, because it contains ions
quiz.rationale: In SiO2 all outer electrons are held in strong covalent bonds throughout the network, so there are no free charge carriers. A lot of energy is needed to break these bonds, giving a very high melting point.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: sentence-frame scaffold for SiO2 (giant covalent) – conductivity and melting point

quiz.prompt: Both diamond and graphite are made only of carbon, yet graphite conducts electricity and diamond does not. What is the best explanation?
choices: Graphite contains metal ions that carry the current
Graphite has more protons in its carbon atoms than diamond
In graphite each carbon forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move along the layer; in diamond all four electrons are held in bonds
Diamond has ions that are locked in place, but graphite has free ions
quiz.rationale: Graphite carbon atoms use only three electrons for bonding in flat layers, leaving one delocalised electron each. In diamond each carbon forms four bonds, so there are no free electrons.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: graphite resolution and cold-call exit question 'why does graphite conduct but diamond does not'

quiz.prompt: Graphite is soft enough to write with, even though the bonds inside each of its layers are strong. Why is it soft?
choices: The layers are held to each other only by weak van der Waals forces, so they slide over each other easily
It has delocalised electrons, which make any solid soft
The covalent bonds inside the layers are weak
Its carbon atoms are bonded in a 3-D tetrahedral network
quiz.rationale: Strong covalent bonds exist only within the layers. The forces between layers are weak van der Waals forces, so layers slide off easily and leave a mark.
quiz.placement: Explain phase: teacher's two-panel diagram of diamond and graphite (layers held by van der Waals forces)

quiz.prompt: A student wrote on a green sticky note: 'NaCl conducts because it is ionic.' What important idea is missing to make this a complete explanation?
choices: NaCl conducts because its molecules carry charge
NaCl conducts because it has delocalised electrons
NaCl conducts only when its ions are free to move, that is, when it is dissolved in water or molten
NaCl conducts in the solid state because the ions move through the crystal
quiz.rationale: Being ionic is not enough. Conduction needs mobile ions, which are only free in solution or in the molten state, not in the solid lattice.
quiz.placement: DQB phase: green 'We Can Now Explain' sticky notes (teacher flags notes missing 'free-moving ions')

quiz.prompt: Which bond type explains the anomalous electrical conductivity of graphite?
choices: Ionic bond
Hydrogen bond
Metallic bond between metal ions
Covalent bond with delocalised electrons
quiz.rationale: Graphite is a giant covalent structure in which each carbon uses three electrons in covalent bonds, and the fourth electron is delocalised along the layer and carries charge.
quiz.placement: Model phase: exit ticket Part 3 (circle the bond type that explains the conductivity of graphite)

lessons.title: Resultant Structures & Uses: From Bond Type to Real-World Application

quiz.prompt: Aluminium foil is used to wrap mandazi and can be pressed into very thin sheets without breaking. Which statement correctly gives the bond type in aluminium and explains why it can be shaped like this?
choices: Covalent bonding: shared electron pairs between two atoms form small molecules that bend easily
Metallic bonding: layers of aluminium atoms can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together
Weak forces between separate aluminium molecules let the foil be shaped easily
Ionic bonding: strong attraction between positive and negative ions makes the foil flexible
quiz.rationale: Aluminium is a metal held by metallic bonding: a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. The layers can slide without the structure breaking, so the metal is malleable.
quiz.placement: Predict: choose ONE of the three objects (aluminium foil, glass bottle, graphite rod) and predict its bond type and properties

quiz.prompt: A graphite rod from a torch (dry-cell) battery carries electric current. Which feature of graphite's structure explains why it conducts electricity?
choices: Each carbon atom is held by four covalent bonds, so electrons move along the bonds
Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that is free to move between the layers
Graphite is made of small molecules that carry charge from one to the next
Graphite contains positive and negative ions that are free to move
quiz.rationale: In graphite each carbon atom forms three bonds in a flat hexagonal layer. The fourth electron is delocalised and free to move, so graphite conducts. The covalent bonds themselves do not carry current.
quiz.placement: Predict: graphite rod from a disassembled size-D dry-cell battery

quiz.prompt: Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) is melted at a very high temperature to make glass for windows. Which statement best explains why SiO₂ has such a very high melting point?
choices: Its positive and negative ions are attracted by weak forces
It has a giant covalent structure, so a huge number of strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
It is made of small molecules held by weak forces that are easy to separate
It has delocalised electrons that make the atoms move apart easily
quiz.rationale: SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure. Every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, so a great deal of energy is needed to break them.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Substance Dossiers (SiO₂ dossier: bond type, structure and melting point)

quiz.prompt: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is rubbed into nyama choma and dissolves in water. It has a high melting point, and solid NaCl does not conduct electricity. Which explanation is correct?
choices: NaCl is an ionic lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by strong attractions; in the solid the ions cannot move, so it does not conduct
NaCl is a giant covalent structure with delocalised electrons that are fixed in place
NaCl is a metallic lattice, but its electrons are held too tightly to move
NaCl is made of small covalent molecules, so it melts easily but conducts poorly
quiz.rationale: NaCl is an ionic compound with a lattice of oppositely charged ions. Strong attractions give a high melting point. In the solid the ions are fixed in position, so there are no mobile charges to carry current.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Substance Dossiers (NaCl dossier: ionic bond type, melting point, conductivity, solubility)

quiz.prompt: A grinding wheel in a Kisumu workshop is made of silicon carbide (SiC). It is extremely hard, has a very high melting point and conducts electricity only very poorly. What is the most likely bond type and structure of SiC?
choices: Giant covalent structure, similar to diamond
Simple molecular structure with weak forces between molecules
Ionic lattice of positive and negative ions
Metallic lattice with a sea of delocalised electrons
quiz.rationale: Extreme hardness, a very high melting point and poor conductivity match a giant covalent structure like diamond. An ionic or metallic structure would not fit this pattern, and a simple molecular structure would be soft with a low melting point.
quiz.placement: Activity B: Kenyan Materials Gallery Walk (Mystery Material X poster)

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon. Why does diamond NOT conduct electricity at all?
choices: All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in covalent bonds, so no electrons are free to move
Diamond has no electrons because it is transparent
Diamond contains ions that are locked in a lattice
Diamond is too hard for electrons to pass through
quiz.rationale: In diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a tetrahedral network. All its outer electrons are used in bonding, so there are no delocalised electrons or ions to carry charge.
quiz.placement: Part A: Pair Presentations (diamond and graphite substance-expert presentations and listening grid)

quiz.prompt: A student says: 'Diamond and graphite behave differently because graphite contains more protons and neutrons than diamond.' Which response is correct?
choices: The student is correct, because graphite has extra electrons that make it conduct
The student is wrong, because both contain only carbon atoms; the difference comes from how the carbon atoms are bonded and arranged
The student is correct, because the number of protons decides how hard a solid is
The student is wrong, because diamond is made of a different element from graphite
quiz.rationale: Both substances are 100% carbon with identical atoms. Diamond has four bonds per atom in a 3-D tetrahedral network, while graphite has three bonds per atom in flat hexagonal layers with one delocalised electron. This is the carbon paradox.
quiz.placement: DQB update: re-reading the driving question and writing green notes on what you can now explain about the carbon paradox

quiz.prompt: A jeweller's tile cutter is tipped with diamond. In a model of diamond, an arrow is drawn from a structural feature to this use. Which structural feature should the arrow start from to explain why diamond can cut tiles?
choices: Delocalised electrons that are free to move
Positive and negative ions held in a lattice
Each carbon atom bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds in a 3-D tetrahedral network
Layers of atoms that slide over each other easily
quiz.rationale: Diamond's hardness comes from every carbon atom being strongly bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network. This makes it hard enough to scratch the ceramic tile.
quiz.placement: Step 1: Uses Annotation (arrows from structural features to Kenyan uses in the cumulative model portfolio)

quiz.prompt: A pencil leaves a grey mark on exam paper, but diamond is used to cut tiles. Which statement best explains the pencil's soft, marking graphite?
choices: Graphite has fewer carbon atoms than diamond
Graphite has four strong bonds per carbon atom in a 3-D network
Graphite is an ionic solid with weak attractions between ions
Graphite is made of flat hexagonal layers that can slide off one another and leave a mark
quiz.rationale: Graphite has a layered structure of flat hexagonal sheets. The layers slide over each other and rub off onto paper, so graphite is soft and useful for writing. Diamond's rigid 3-D network does not allow this.
quiz.placement: Step 2: Comparison Panel, 'The Carbon Paradox — Explained' (diamond vs graphite properties and Kenyan uses)

lessons.title: Animations, Simulations & Digital Literacy: Seeing Chemical Bonding in Motion

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. In diamond, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to, and how are the atoms arranged?
choices: Four, in flat layers held together by weak forces
Two, in long single chains
Three, in flat hexagonal layers
Four, in a 3-D tetrahedral network
quiz.rationale: Each carbon in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds to four neighbours, giving a rigid 3-D tetrahedral network. Three bonds in flat hexagonal layers describes graphite.
quiz.placement: Phase 1: Digital Prediction Card (retrieval sketching of diamond, graphite and the NaCl lattice)

quiz.prompt: A learner watches an animation of graphite and sees electrons moving along the layers. Which statement correctly explains why these free electrons are there?
choices: Graphite is black, and black substances always contain free electrons
All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are used in bonds, so the electrons shown are extra ones from outside
Each carbon atom gives away one electron to form C⁺ ions arranged in a lattice
Each carbon atom uses three outer electrons in bonds, and the fourth is delocalised and free to move along the layer
quiz.rationale: In graphite each carbon forms three bonds within its hexagonal layer. The fourth outer electron is delocalised and can move along the layer, which is why graphite conducts electricity.
quiz.placement: Station 2: Giant Covalent Structures (Diamond & Graphite), animation of graphite's layered structure

quiz.prompt: In an animation of sodium chloride (NaCl) forming, what happens to the valence electron of each sodium atom?
choices: It stays on sodium and becomes delocalised among all the sodium atoms
It is shared equally between the sodium and chlorine atoms
It is transferred to a chlorine atom, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other
It is lost completely and not taken up by any other atom
quiz.rationale: Sodium transfers one valence electron to chlorine, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Their electrostatic attraction builds the lattice and explains the high melting point.
quiz.placement: Station 1: Ionic Bonding (NaCl lattice) animation

quiz.prompt: An electron-sea animation of aluminium shows a lattice of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons. How does this explain why aluminium conducts electricity?
choices: The delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry charge
The metal contains Al³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that move when a voltage is applied
The positive ions move through the metal and carry the charge
The metal atoms share electrons in fixed pairs, which pass charge along the bonds
quiz.rationale: In metallic bonding the positive ions stay in fixed positions while the delocalised electrons move freely, so they carry electric charge through the metal.
quiz.placement: Station 3: Metallic Bonding (Aluminium) electron-sea animation

quiz.prompt: In the solubility investigation, NaCl dissolved in water but SiO₂ (sand) did not. Which explanation matches what the simulations showed?
choices: SiO₂ has delocalised electrons, which stop it from dissolving
NaCl has weak bonds, but SiO₂ has no bonds at all
NaCl is an ionic lattice that water can pull apart into ions, while SiO₂ is a giant covalent network of strong bonds that water cannot break
NaCl is a giant covalent network and SiO₂ is an ionic lattice
quiz.rationale: Water molecules can pull Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions out of the ionic lattice. The strong covalent bonds throughout SiO₂ cannot be broken by water, so sand stays undissolved.
quiz.placement: Discussion Question 2: NaCl simulation vs. SiO₂ in the solubility investigation

quiz.prompt: In the conductivity test, graphite lit the bulb but diamond did not. Why does diamond not conduct electricity?
choices: Diamond atoms have fewer protons than graphite atoms
All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are held in bonds, so there are no free electrons to carry charge
Diamond is transparent, so charge passes straight through without stopping
Diamond is too hard for electricity to enter it
quiz.rationale: In diamond each carbon uses all four outer electrons in strong covalent bonds, so no electrons are free to move. Diamond and graphite have the same number of protons because both are pure carbon.
quiz.placement: Discussion Question 1: graphite simulation vs. conductivity results of graphite and diamond

quiz.prompt: A learner adds a 'Model Limitations' box to their bonding model. Which entry names a real limitation of a bonding simulation?
choices: Simulations show electrons as dots, but real electrons behave more like probability clouds
Simulations show that diamond and graphite have different numbers of protons
Simulations prove that chemical bonds do not really exist
Simulations cannot show any structure of a substance
quiz.rationale: All models simplify reality. Showing electrons as dots is a simplification of their quantum behaviour. The other statements are false, since bonds exist, both substances are pure carbon, and simulations do show structures.
quiz.placement: Model revision: adding a 'Model Limitations' box to the Carbon Bonding Model

lessons.title: Project Lesson — 3-D Model Building: Bonding Structures with Locally Available Materials

quiz.prompt: A group is planning a 3-D model of diamond. Each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. Which bond angle should the group write on their blueprint?
quiz.rationale: The four bonds around each carbon in diamond point to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving a bond angle of 109.5°. A 90° angle is the common error the teacher checks for on blueprint sheets.
quiz.placement: Model Blueprint Sheet: planning prompt (2) on the bond angle(s) the model must show

quiz.prompt: A group builds a sodium chloride (NaCl) model by alternating two colours of clay in a 3-D grid. How many Cl⁻ ions should surround each Na⁺ ion in the finished model?
quiz.rationale: In the NaCl ionic lattice each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by 6 Na⁺ ions, so the coordination number is 6:6.
quiz.placement: Build phase: NaCl group alternating two clay colours and counting that each Na⁺ is surrounded by 6 Cl⁻

quiz.prompt: In a graphite model, carbon atoms in a layer are joined by rigid wire, but the layers are joined only by loose string. When you pull the layers apart, what do the loose strings represent breaking?
choices: Metallic bonds between the carbon atoms
Strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms in the same layer
Ionic bonds between the layers
Weak Van der Waals forces between the layers
quiz.rationale: Only weak Van der Waals forces hold the layers together, so the layers slide over each other easily. This is why graphite is soft and leaves a mark on paper. The strong covalent bonds inside each layer stay intact.
quiz.placement: Build phase: graphite group connecting layers with loose string to represent weak Van der Waals forces

quiz.prompt: A student building the SiO₂ model connects each central maize-kernel 'Si' to beans representing 'O' atoms, and then bridges the oxygens to the next Si. How should each Si atom be bonded in a correct SiO₂ giant covalent lattice?
choices: To two O atoms in a straight line
To three O atoms in a flat layer
To four O atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement
To six O atoms, like Na⁺ in NaCl
quiz.rationale: In SiO₂ each Si is covalently bonded to four O atoms arranged tetrahedrally, and each O links to another Si. This builds a giant covalent lattice.
quiz.placement: Build phase: SiO₂ group connecting each central maize-kernel 'Si' to four bean 'O' atoms

quiz.prompt: During the carousel, a visitor writes on a graphite model: 'Graphite conducts electricity because it has metal in it.' Which comment on the peer review card would correct this?
choices: Graphite conducts because its layers are held together by weak Van der Waals forces.
Graphite conducts because it has four bonds per carbon atom, like diamond.
Graphite conducts because each carbon has one delocalised electron free to move along the layers.
Graphite conducts because it is an ionic lattice with free ions.
quiz.rationale: Each carbon in graphite uses three electrons in bonding, leaving one delocalised electron that can move and carry charge. Graphite contains only carbon, with no metal.
quiz.placement: Peer review carousel: teacher listening at the diamond and graphite models for the misconception 'it has metal in it'

quiz.prompt: Both diamond and graphite are 100% carbon. Why does the diamond model fit a material that is extremely hard and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft and conducts?
choices: Diamond is an ionic compound and graphite is a covalent compound.
Diamond has four bonds per carbon in a 3-D tetrahedral network, while graphite has three bonds per carbon in layers with weak forces between them.
Diamond contains a metal that holds the atoms together, while graphite does not.
Diamond has more protons in its carbon atoms than graphite.
quiz.rationale: The two materials contain the same atoms, so the difference is the bonding arrangement. Diamond's 3-D network of four bonds locks every atom in place. Graphite's layers of three bonds per atom are weakly held together and leave one electron free.
quiz.placement: Whole-class question at the diamond and graphite models: 'why is one the hardest substance on Earth and the other writes on paper?'

quiz.prompt: A student completes the sticky note: 'I can now explain why diamond does not conduct electricity because I built the tetrahedral model and saw that ______.' Which ending is correct?
choices: the layers are held together by only loose string
every carbon electron is locked in a covalent bond, so there are no free electrons
each carbon has one delocalised electron that is trapped between layers
there are free ions that cannot move in the solid
quiz.rationale: Each carbon in diamond uses all four outer electrons in covalent bonds, so no electrons are free to carry charge. This makes diamond an electrical insulator.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board sticky note: 'I can now explain ______ about the carbon paradox because I built ______'

lessons.title: Model Presentations, Driving Question Board Final Revision and Unit Consolidation

quiz.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms. Diamond does not conduct electricity at all. Which statement best explains why?
choices: Diamond has delocalised electrons, but they are trapped between layers
Each carbon atom uses all four outer electrons in strong covalent bonds, so no electrons are free to move
Diamond atoms have no electrons
Diamond has ionic bonds, and ionic solids never conduct
quiz.rationale: In diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds in a tetrahedral network, so all outer electrons are held in bonds. With no free-moving charged particles, diamond cannot conduct.
quiz.placement: Predict callback: written explanation of the Carbon Paradox (diamond and graphite samples)

quiz.prompt: Graphite from a pencil lights a bulb when connected in a circuit. Which feature of its structure explains this?
choices: Each carbon atom forms four bonds in a tetrahedral network
Graphite contains metal atoms mixed in with the carbon
Each carbon atom forms three bonds in flat hexagonal layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move
Graphite is made of positive and negative ions that move when connected
quiz.rationale: Each carbon in graphite uses only three outer electrons for bonding in hexagonal layers. The fourth electron is delocalised and carries charge through the layers.
quiz.placement: Predict callback: written explanation of the Carbon Paradox (diamond and graphite samples)

quiz.prompt: A group presents a 3-D model of a sodium chloride (NaCl) lattice. Which description of the bonding and a matching property is correct?
choices: Van der Waals forces: weak forces between ions make NaCl soft and easy to melt
Ionic bonds: strong attractions between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice give a high melting point
Covalent bonds: shared electron pairs between separate NaCl molecules give a low melting point
Metallic bonds: a sea of delocalised electrons lets solid NaCl conduct electricity
quiz.rationale: NaCl is a giant ionic lattice. Many strong electrostatic attractions between Na+ and Cl- ions need a lot of energy to break, so the melting point is high.
quiz.placement: Model presentations: NaCl ionic lattice group presentation and gallery walk

quiz.prompt: Silicon dioxide (SiO2), the main compound in sand used in construction, is a continuous network of atoms joined by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. In the class comparison table, which structure type does it belong to, and why?
choices: Giant metallic, because it is hard and has a high melting point
Simple molecular, because it is made of covalent bonds
Giant covalent, because strong covalent bonds link all the atoms in one continuous network
Giant ionic, because it contains a metal and a non-metal
quiz.rationale: A substance whose atoms are all joined by covalent bonds in a continuous network is giant covalent, like diamond. It is not simple molecular, because there are no small separate molecules.
quiz.placement: Whole-class consolidation: completing the unit comparison table (giant covalent row)

quiz.prompt: Graphite is soft enough to write with, even though the bonds between carbon atoms inside each layer are strong. What explains this?
choices: The covalent bonds inside the layers are weaker than those in diamond
Graphite has fewer protons than diamond
The delocalised electrons break the layers apart when pressed
Each layer is held to the next by weak Van der Waals forces, so layers slide off easily
quiz.rationale: Strong covalent bonds hold atoms within a layer. Only weak Van der Waals forces hold the layers together, so layers slide and rub off onto paper.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board final revision: answering the graphite and pencil question with evidence

quiz.prompt: An aluminium sufuria (cooking pot) heats up quickly on a jiko and food cooks evenly. Which property of metallic bonding best explains why the metal conducts heat well?
choices: Metal atoms share electrons in fixed pairs between two atoms only
A sea of delocalised electrons moves freely through the lattice of metal ions and carries energy
Weak Van der Waals forces between layers let heat pass through
Positive and negative ions are held in a rigid lattice with no free particles
quiz.rationale: Metals have delocalised electrons that move freely among positive metal ions. They carry thermal energy quickly, which makes metals suitable for cookware.
quiz.placement: Exit ticket: Section 3, property to use (Kenyan context)

quiz.prompt: Which statement is the best three-part summary of the Carbon Paradox for diamond and graphite?
choices: Diamond has more protons than graphite, so it is harder and does not conduct
Graphite has more electrons than diamond, so it conducts
Diamond has ionic bonds and graphite has covalent bonds, so their properties differ
Both contain only carbon, but diamond has four bonds per atom in a 3-D network, while graphite has three bonds per atom in layers with one delocalised electron, so their properties differ
quiz.rationale: Diamond and graphite have identical atoms. The difference in properties comes only from how the atoms are bonded: a tetrahedral network in diamond, and layers with delocalised electrons in graphite.
quiz.placement: Exit ticket: Section 4, The Carbon Paradox (three-sentence explanation)
